The National Statistical Office (NSO / NSSO) measures unemployment using UPS, UPSS, CWS, and CDS approaches.
Under Current Weekly Status (CWS), working just 1 hour during the reference week classifies an individual as employed.
Educated unemployment is driven by an academic curriculum disconnected from industry-demanded technical skills.

quizPool.question: What is the defining economic characteristic of 'Disguised Unemployment'?
options: Workers wear disguises to receive multiple salaries
Marginal productivity of the surplus workers is zero or near zero
Workers are employed exclusively during midnight shifts
Wages paid exceed the company's total annual turnover
quizPool.explanation: Disguised unemployment occurs when more people are engaged in an activity (commonly family farming) than required, meaning removing a worker causes zero drop in total output.

quizPool.question: Which form of unemployment arises due to a long-term mismatch between the skills workers possess and the skills required by modern industry?
quizPool.explanation: Structural unemployment occurs when technological transformation or economic evolution renders existing worker qualifications outdated for new job vacancies.

quizPool.question: Under the NSSO Current Weekly Status (CWS) criterion, a person is considered employed if they worked for at least:
options: 1 hour on any one day during the 7-day reference week
6 full days in the reference week
365 continuous days in the preceding year
quizPool.explanation: Under the Current Weekly Status (CWS) approach, an individual is recorded as employed if they performed gainful work for at least one hour on any single day in the preceding 7 days.

quizPool.question: What does the Worker Population Ratio (WPR) measure?
options: The percentage of total population that is actively employed in productive work
The ratio of retired citizens to active university students
The total number of factories operating in an industrial district
The percentage of workers enrolled in trade unions
quizPool.explanation: Worker Population Ratio (WPR) is defined as the percentage of employed persons in the total population, reflecting the economy's employment-generating capacity.

quizPool.question: Which agency under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) conducts the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) in India?
options: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
quizPool.explanation: The National Statistical Office (NSO, formerly NSSO) conducts the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) to assess employment and unemployment trends across India.

summary.overview: Comprehensive macroeconomic analysis of Module 5: Open-Ended Contemporary Issues in Indian Economy. Covers fiscal deficit definitions, components and historical trends, the FRBM Act consolidation roadmap, pandemic fiscal shocks, inflation types (demand-pull vs cost-push), price indices (WPI vs CPI Combined), and the RBI Flexible Inflation Targeting monetary policy framework.

sections.title: Fiscal Deficit: Concepts, Components & Mathematical Formulations
points: Fiscal Deficit Definition: The excess of total government expenditure over total non-debt receipts (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts such as loan recoveries and disinvestment proceeds).
Economic Significance: Reflects the total borrowing requirements of the central government from internal and external sources to bridge the budgetary gap.
Revenue Deficit: The excess of total revenue expenditure over total revenue receipts; reflects government borrowing to finance day-to-day consumption rather than capital assets.

Primary Deficit: Fiscal Deficit minus interest payments on past debt: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit - Interest Payments. Measures the current fiscal stance excluding legacy debt servicing obligations.

sections.title: Fiscal Deficit Trends in India & Pandemic Shocks
points: Pre-Pandemic Benchmark: India maintained central fiscal deficits around 3.4% to 4.5% of GDP in compliance with post-2010 consolidation trajectories.
COVID-19 Pandemic Surge: In FY2020–21, the fiscal deficit spiked to 9.2% of GDP (₹18.2 lakh crore) due to emergency healthcare spending, free food grains (PM-GKAY), and revenue contraction.
Consolidation Roadmap: Government adopted a Glide Path reducing fiscal deficit to 6.71% (FY22), 6.4% (FY23), 5.6% (FY24), 4.8% (FY25), and targeting 4.4% of GDP by FY2025–26.

Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act 2003: Originally mandated reducing fiscal deficit to 3% of GDP and eliminating revenue deficit; N.K. Singh Committee (2017) recommended targeting a general government debt-to-GDP ratio of 60% (40% central, 20% state).

sections.title: Inflation Dynamics: Demand-Pull vs. Cost-Push Drivers
points: Inflation Definition: A sustained and persistent rise in the general price level across an economy, eroding the domestic purchasing power of money.
Demand-Pull Inflation: Occurs when aggregate demand for goods and services outpaces aggregate supply ('too much money chasing too few goods'); common during post-pandemic consumption recoveries.
Cost-Push Inflation: Caused by sharp increases in production costs, wages, or imported raw materials (such as global crude oil spikes and shipping freight disruptions).
Core vs. Headline Inflation: Headline inflation includes volatile food and energy prices; Core inflation strips out food and fuel to measure underlying persistent price pressure.

sections.title: Price Indices & Monetary Policy Framework: WPI vs. CPI Combined
points: Wholesale Price Index (WPI): Published by Ministry of Commerce and Industry; base year 2011–12; heavily weighted toward manufactured goods (~64.2%) and primary articles (~22.6%); completely excludes services.

Consumer Price Index (CPI Combined): Published by NSO (MoSPI); base year 2012; measures retail price inflation across consumer baskets; food & beverages represent ~45.86%; includes services (housing, education, health, transport).
Monetary Policy Anchor: Following the Urjit Patel Committee recommendations (2014), the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) officially abandoned WPI and adopted CPI Combined as its headline inflation anchor.
Flexible Inflation Targeting (FIT): Statutory mandate requiring RBI's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) to maintain headline CPI inflation at 4% with a permissible tolerance band of ± 2% (2% to 6%).

The FRBM Act of 2003 established the benchmark 3% of GDP ceiling for the central fiscal deficit.
RBI uses CPI Combined rather than WPI because CPI incorporates services and directly measures retail living costs.
The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) targets 4% inflation within a statutory tolerance band of 2% to 6%.

quizPool.question: How is the Primary Deficit mathematically calculated in public finance?
quizPool.explanation: Primary Deficit is Fiscal Deficit minus interest payments on past borrowings, showing the fiscal gap generated exclusively by current government policy.

quizPool.question: What key benchmark was set by the original Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act of 2003 for the central fiscal deficit?
options: Reduce Fiscal Deficit to 3% of GDP
Increase Fiscal Deficit to 15% of GDP
Maintain zero government expenditure on defense
Borrow exclusively from foreign central banks
quizPool.explanation: The FRBM Act enacted in 2003 mandated reducing the gross fiscal deficit of the central government to 3% of GDP to maintain long-term macroeconomic stability.

quizPool.question: Which price index is officially adopted by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as the headline anchor for monetary policy and inflation targeting?
quizPool.explanation: Following the Urjit Patel Committee recommendations, the RBI adopted the Consumer Price Index (CPI) Combined as the key metric for monetary policy and inflation targeting.

quizPool.question: What is the statutory inflation target mandated to the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of the Reserve Bank of India?
options: 4% with a tolerance band of +/- 2% (2% to 6%)
Variable inflation set by international crude prices
quizPool.explanation: Under the flexible inflation targeting framework, the MPC is mandated to maintain headline CPI inflation at 4% with a permissible tolerance band between 2% and 6%.

quizPool.question: What is 'Cost-Push Inflation' primarily caused by?
options: Sudden increases in production costs, such as imported crude oil shocks or raw material price spikes
Excessive money printing by the treasury causing consumer shopping frenzies
A universal reduction in all corporate tax rates
A massive drop in global freight transport fees
quizPool.explanation: Cost-push inflation occurs when aggregate supply decreases due to higher costs of inputs, wages, or imported raw materials like petroleum, pushing prices upward.
